name: Sternocleidomastoid
inDailyLife: Turning your head to look over your shoulder
Tipping your ear toward your shoulder
Lifting your head off a pillow
Helping you breathe in during hard effort
whenWeak: Turning to check traffic may feel tiring or stiff
Lifting your head from lying down can feel harder
quickFacts: It runs from behind the ear to the collarbone and breastbone.
You have one on each side of the neck.

name: Pectoralis major (chest)
inDailyLife: Pushing a door or a heavy cart forward
Pushing yourself up from the floor or a chair
Hugging someone or bringing your arms together
Throwing a ball overhand
whenWeak: Pushing doors or getting up from the floor may feel harder
Carrying a load in front of your chest can tire your arms sooner
quickFacts: It has three parts that fan out from the collarbone, breastbone and ribs.
It pulls the upper arm toward the middle of your body.

name: Pectoralis minor
inDailyLife: Reaching forward to grab something
Rolling your shoulders forward
Helping you breathe in deeply
Holding your shoulder blade steady as you lean on your hands
whenWeak: Shoulders may feel less steady when you reach forward
Deep breaths may feel a bit more effortful
quickFacts: It is a small, flat muscle that lies under the large chest muscle.
It connects the shoulder blade to the ribs.

name: Serratus anterior
inDailyLife: Reaching up to a high shelf
Pushing a heavy door open with your arm out
Keeping your shoulder blade flat against your ribs
Throwing or swinging an arm forward
whenWeak: Lifting an arm overhead may feel less smooth
Your shoulder blade may stick out at the back when you push
quickFacts: It wraps around the side of the ribs like fingers.
It is often called the boxer's muscle because it helps your arm reach forward.

name: External oblique
inDailyLife: Twisting to reach the seat belt
Bending sideways to pick up a bag
Coughing, sneezing or laughing hard
Keeping your trunk steady while you walk
whenWeak: Twisting around may feel stiff or weak
Your middle may feel less steady when you carry a bag on one side
quickFacts: It is the largest and outermost of the side belly muscles.
Its fibres run downward and inward, like sliding your hands into front pockets.

name: Internal oblique
inDailyLife: Twisting to look behind you in a chair
Bracing when you cough or lift a box
Bending sideways to tie a shoe
Helping you breathe out forcefully
whenWeak: Twisting and bracing may feel less controlled
Your trunk may feel wobbly when you carry something heavy
quickFacts: It lies under the external oblique with fibres running the other way.
It helps turn your trunk to the same side.

name: Rectus abdominis (abs)
inDailyLife: Sitting up from lying down
Bending forward to pick something up
Keeping your ribs and hips in line as you stand
Breathing out hard when you cough
whenWeak: Sitting up from bed may take more effort
Standing tall for long may feel tiring
quickFacts: It is the long muscle down the front of the belly, often called the abs.
The ridges you may see are bands of tissue that cross the muscle.

name: Transversus abdominis
inDailyLife: Bracing your middle before you lift a heavy bag
Coughing, sneezing or laughing
Helping hold your organs in place
Steadying your trunk as you stand up
whenWeak: Your middle may feel less supported when you lift
Your lower back may tire sooner when you carry things
quickFacts: It is the deepest belly muscle and wraps around you like a belt.
It does not move your spine much; it mostly holds your trunk steady.

name: Latissimus dorsi (lats)
inDailyLife: Pulling a heavy door open
Climbing a ladder
Pulling a seat belt across you
Pushing up from armrests when you stand
whenWeak: Pulling things toward you may feel harder
Reaching overhead may feel less strong
quickFacts: It is the widest muscle of the back and spans from the spine to the upper arm.
It pulls the arm down and back toward your body.

name: Multifidus
inDailyLife: Keeping your spine steady as you walk
Standing up straight after bending
Holding your back stable when you carry bags
Sitting upright at a desk
whenWeak: Your back may tire quickly when you stand for long
Bending and straightening may feel less smooth
quickFacts: It is a deep muscle with short bundles that run along the spine.
Each bundle spans only a few bones, so it fine-tunes small spine movements.

name: Erector spinae (back extensors)
inDailyLife: Standing up straight after bending down
Lifting a child or a bag from the floor
Leaning back to look at the ceiling
Holding your trunk upright while you walk
whenWeak: Standing tall for a long time may feel tiring
Straightening up after bending may feel stiff or slow
quickFacts: It is a group of long muscles that run along both sides of the spine.
It reaches from the pelvis up toward the neck.

name: Trapezius, upper
inDailyLife: Shrugging your shoulders
Carrying a heavy bag on your shoulder
Holding a phone between ear and shoulder
Looking up or tilting your head back
whenWeak: Carrying bags may tire your shoulders sooner
Lifting your shoulders may feel weak
quickFacts: It is the top part of the large kite-shaped muscle across the upper back.
It lifts the shoulder blade and helps tilt the head.

name: Trapezius, middle and lower
inDailyLife: Pulling your shoulders back to stand tall
Reaching overhead to a high shelf
Holding your arms out while you drive
Hanging a coat on a high hook
whenWeak: Your shoulders may drift forward when you sit
Lifting arms overhead may feel less smooth
quickFacts: These fibres pull the shoulder blade toward the spine and downward.
The lower part is shaped like a triangle pointing down the spine.

name: Rhomboids
inDailyLife: Pulling your shoulder blades together
Keeping your shoulders from rolling forward
Pulling a heavy door toward you
Lowering your arm from a high shelf
whenWeak: Your upper back may feel rounded or tired when you sit
Pulling movements may feel less steady
quickFacts: They lie under the trapezius between your spine and shoulder blade.
There are two, rhomboid major and rhomboid minor.

name: Levator scapulae
inDailyLife: Shrugging a shoulder up
Turning your head to look to the side
Tilting your head toward one shoulder
Carrying a bag on one shoulder
whenWeak: Your neck and shoulder may feel tight after long desk time
Turning your head may feel stiff
quickFacts: The name means lifter of the shoulder blade.
It runs from the top of the neck bones to the top of the shoulder blade.

name: Deltoid (shoulder cap)
inDailyLife: Raising your arm to reach a shelf
Lifting a bag away from your body
Pushing a door open
Reaching behind you to put on a coat
whenWeak: Lifting your arm out to the side may feel harder
Reaching overhead may tire you sooner
quickFacts: It has three parts: front, side and back.
It gives the shoulder its rounded cap shape.

name: Rotator cuff
inDailyLife: Throwing a ball
Reaching behind you to tuck in a shirt
Brushing or combing your hair
Holding your shoulder joint steady while you lift
whenWeak: Lifting your arm overhead may feel weak or less smooth
Reaching behind your back may feel harder
quickFacts: It is four small muscles that hold the arm bone in the shoulder socket.
They are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis.

name: Teres major
inDailyLife: Pulling your arm down and back
Reaching back for a seat belt
Pushing yourself up from armrests
Turning your arm inward
whenWeak: Pulling your arm down may feel weaker
Reaching behind you may feel harder
quickFacts: It is sometimes called the lat's little helper.
It runs from the lower shoulder blade to the upper arm bone.

name: Biceps brachii
inDailyLife: Lifting a grocery bag
Carrying a box with bent arms
Turning a door handle or screwdriver
Bringing a cup to your mouth
Pulling a door open
whenWeak: Carrying bags with bent arms may tire you sooner
Turning a screwdriver may feel weaker
quickFacts: Biceps means two heads; it has a long head and a short head.
It bends the elbow and turns the palm up.

name: Brachialis
inDailyLife: Lifting a bag with your palm facing down
Bending your elbow to carry a box
Lowering a heavy item slowly
Holding a bag steady
whenWeak: Elbow bending may feel weaker with a load
Carrying shopping may tire your arms sooner
quickFacts: It lies under the biceps and is the main elbow bender.
It works whichever way your palm faces.

name: Coracobrachialis
inDailyLife: Lifting your arm forward
Bringing your arm across your body
Reaching forward to pick something up
Swinging your arms when you walk
whenWeak: Lifting your arm forward may feel less strong
Moving your arm across your body may feel weaker
quickFacts: It is a small muscle on the inner upper arm.
It runs from the shoulder blade to the middle of the arm bone.

name: Triceps brachii
inDailyLife: Straightening your arm to push a door
Pushing yourself up from a chair
Reaching to put something on a shelf
Throwing a ball
Pushing a shopping cart
whenWeak: Pushing yourself up from a chair may feel harder
Reaching overhead may tire your arms
quickFacts: Triceps means three heads: long, lateral and medial.
It is the main muscle that straightens the elbow.

name: Brachioradialis
inDailyLife: Lifting a cup with your thumb up
Hammering or stirring
Carrying a bag by a handle
Opening a jar
whenWeak: Lifting with a thumb-up hand may feel weaker
Stirring or hammering may tire your forearm sooner
quickFacts: It sits on the thumb side of the forearm.
It helps bend the elbow when your thumb points up.

name: Forearm extensors (back of forearm)
inDailyLife: Lifting your wrist and hand back
Typing on a keyboard
Opening your fingers to let go of an object
Holding your wrist steady when you grip
whenWeak: Your wrist may tire when you type or grip
Letting go of objects may feel less smooth
quickFacts: They sit on the back of the forearm and run to the wrist and fingers.
They work with the front forearm muscles to keep the wrist steady when you grip.

name: Forearm flexors (front of forearm)
meshKeys: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
inDailyLife: Gripping a handle or a bag
Opening a jar
Writing or using a phone
Bending your wrist toward your palm
Shaking hands
whenWeak: Your grip may tire sooner when you carry things
Opening jars may feel harder
quickFacts: They sit on the palm side of the forearm.
Their tendons run through the wrist to the fingers.

name: Pronator teres
inDailyLife: Turning your palm to face down
Pouring from a jug
Turning a key
Turning a door handle
whenWeak: Turning your palm down may feel weaker
Pouring from a heavy jug may feel awkward
quickFacts: Pronate means to turn the palm down.
It runs diagonally from the inner elbow across the forearm.

name: Gluteus maximus
inDailyLife: Standing up from a chair or toilet
Climbing stairs or a steep hill
Walking uphill
Getting out of a car
Pushing off when you run
whenWeak: Climbing stairs may feel harder
Standing up from a low seat may take more effort
quickFacts: It is the largest muscle in the body.
It pushes your thigh back and turns it outward.

name: Gluteus medius and minimus
inDailyLife: Standing on one leg while you put on trousers
Keeping your hips level as you walk
Stepping sideways
Stepping onto a curb
whenWeak: Balancing on one leg may feel wobbly
Your hips may sway more when you walk
quickFacts: They sit on the side of the hip.
Gluteus minimus lies under gluteus medius.

name: Tensor fasciae latae
inDailyLife: Lifting your knee to step up
Stepping sideways
Swinging your leg forward while you walk
Keeping your hip steady when you stand on one leg
whenWeak: Stepping up may feel less smooth
The outer hip may feel tired after a long walk
quickFacts: It is a small muscle at the front and side of the hip.
It connects to the iliotibial band, a long strip of tissue down the outer thigh.

name: Iliopsoas (deep hip flexor)
inDailyLife: Lifting your knee to climb stairs
Stepping over a bump or a curb
Sitting up from lying down
Swinging your leg forward as you walk
Getting your leg into a car
whenWeak: Stairs may feel harder
Lifting your leg to step over things may feel heavy
quickFacts: It is the main hip flexor, made of two muscles: iliacus and psoas major.
It links your lower spine to your thigh bone.

name: Sartorius
inDailyLife: Crossing one leg over the other
Sitting with an ankle on the opposite knee
Lifting your knee to step up
Sitting cross-legged on the floor
whenWeak: Crossing your legs may feel less easy
Turning your leg outward may feel harder
quickFacts: It is the longest muscle in the body.
Its name comes from the Latin word for tailor, as tailors sat cross-legged.

name: Adductors (inner thigh)
inDailyLife: Squeezing your knees together
Getting in and out of a car
Stepping sideways without wobbling
Riding a bike or a horse
Keeping your legs steady when you walk
whenWeak: Getting out of a car may feel awkward
Your legs may feel less steady when you step sideways
quickFacts: They make up the inner thigh and pull the leg toward the middle.
There are six muscles in this group, as shown here.

name: Rectus femoris
inDailyLife: Kicking a ball
Lifting your knee to climb stairs
Straightening your knee as you stand
Walking up a slope
whenWeak: Climbing stairs may feel harder
Lifting your knee may tire you sooner
quickFacts: It is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip.
It both bends the hip and straightens the knee.

name: Vastus muscles (front thigh)
inDailyLife: Standing up from a chair
Walking down stairs or a ramp
Getting up off the floor
Crouching to pick something up
whenWeak: Standing up from low seats may feel harder
Walking downstairs may feel less steady
quickFacts: There are three: lateral, intermediate and medial.
Together with rectus femoris they form the quadriceps.

name: Hamstrings
inDailyLife: Bending your knee to put on a sock
Slowing your leg down when you walk or run
Leaning forward to pick something up
Pushing off when you walk fast
whenWeak: Leaning forward to pick things up may feel strained
Walking or running fast may tire your legs sooner
quickFacts: They run down the back of the thigh and include the biceps femoris and semimembranosus.
They bend the knee and help straighten the hip.

name: Gastrocnemius (calf)
inDailyLife: Rising onto your toes to reach a shelf
Walking, running and jumping
Pushing off the pedal when you ride
Climbing stairs
whenWeak: Rising onto your toes may feel hard
Walking uphill may tire your calves sooner
quickFacts: It is the larger, rounder calf muscle you can see.
It crosses both the knee and the ankle.

name: Soleus
inDailyLife: Standing for a long time
Walking at an easy pace
Keeping your balance as you sway
Pushing off on every step
whenWeak: Standing for a long time may feel tiring
Your lower legs may tire during long walks
quickFacts: It lies under the gastrocnemius.
It has many slow-twitch fibres, suited to long, steady work.

name: Tibialis anterior (shin)
inDailyLife: Lifting your toes so your foot clears the ground
Walking on your heels
Landing your foot softly as you step
Keeping your balance on uneven ground
whenWeak: Your toes may catch on the ground when you walk
Your foot may slap down when you step
quickFacts: It runs along the front of the shin.
It pulls your foot up toward your shin.

name: Fibularis (outer lower leg)
inDailyLife: Keeping your ankle steady on uneven ground
Turning your foot outward
Balancing on one foot
Stepping off a curb
whenWeak: Your ankle may feel wobbly on uneven ground
Balancing on one foot may feel harder
quickFacts: They run down the outer side of the lower leg.
The older name is peroneus, and you may still see it used.
